optionRationales.text: Pushing further into an active trauma response can retraumatize and is well outside coaching.
Helping them reorient and referring to a trauma professional puts safety and scope first.
Labeling PTSD and prescribing techniques is diagnosis and treatment — not a coach’s role.
Barreling on ignores a person in genuine distress right in front of you.

scenario: A client is in the acute early stage of grief after losing their spouse and is struggling to function.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Coach them to set goals and move on
Acknowledge the grief, recognize this may call for grief counseling, and offer a referral while adjusting your support
Tell them coaching isn’t meant for people who are sad
Take on the role of their grief counselor yourself

explanation.best: Acknowledging the grief and offering a counseling referral is BEST — acute grief support can exceed coaching.
explanation.worst: Acting as their grief counselor is WORST because counseling is a distinct profession outside coaching.

deeperInsight: Coaches recognize when a client’s need is counseling and refer, rather than taking on a clinical role.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you distinguish coaching from counseling and refer for acute grief.

optionRationales.text: Pushing goals during acute grief can feel dismissive of what the client is actually going through.
Acknowledging the grief and offering a referral meets the person where they are, within scope.
Implying coaching isn’t for "sad" people is both unkind and a mischaracterization of coaching.
Stepping into the grief-counselor role takes on a clinical profession that isn’t coaching.

scenario: A client asks you point-blank whether they should sue their employer.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Give your opinion on whether they should sue
Stay in the coaching role, explore what matters to them, and note that legal advice belongs with a qualified attorney
Walk them through exactly how to file the lawsuit
Tell them lawsuits never work out

explanation.best: Staying in the coaching role and directing legal questions to an attorney is BEST — legal advice is outside a coach’s scope.
explanation.worst: Walking them through how to file is WORST because giving legal procedure is well beyond coaching.

deeperInsight: Coaching explores what matters to the client; specific legal, medical, or financial advice is referred to the right professional.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you keep legal questions within the client’s own reflection and refer for expert advice.

optionRationales.text: Offering your opinion on suing steps into legal advice you’re not positioned to give.
Exploring what matters and referring legal specifics to an attorney holds the coaching boundary.
Coaching a client through filing a lawsuit is giving legal counsel — squarely out of scope.
"Lawsuits never work out" is both an unfounded opinion and a nudge that isn’t coaching.

scenario: A client mentions their drinking is affecting their work and relationships and feels out of their control.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Coach them to cut back with accountability goals
Express care, recognize this may exceed coaching, and discuss a referral to appropriate support
Tell them they’re an alcoholic and must go to rehab
Steer away from the topic to keep things positive

explanation.best: Expressing care and discussing a referral is BEST — a possible substance problem can exceed coaching’s scope.
explanation.worst: Labeling them an alcoholic and prescribing rehab is WORST because it diagnoses and directs treatment.

deeperInsight: When a concern points to a possible clinical issue, coaches respond with care and referral, not diagnosis.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you recognize a possible substance issue as beyond coaching and refer with care.

optionRationales.text: Accountability goals may not touch what could be a dependency that needs specialized help.
Care plus a referral honors the client and the limits of coaching.
Diagnosing "alcoholic" and ordering rehab is clinical judgment a coach shouldn’t make.
Avoiding the topic abandons the client on something they named as serious.

scenario: A client expects you to deliver a structured curriculum and teach them leadership frameworks.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Become their instructor and deliver lectures
Clarify what coaching is and, if they want training, refer or offer it as a distinct service while keeping coaching client-led
Present the lectures as though they were coaching
Tell them frameworks are useless

explanation.best: Clarifying coaching versus training and separating the two is BEST — teaching a curriculum is not coaching.
explanation.worst: Passing lectures off as coaching is WORST because it misrepresents the service the client is buying.

deeperInsight: Training transfers the trainer’s content; coaching draws out the client’s own thinking — the distinction is named, not hidden.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you distinguish coaching from training/teaching.

optionRationales.text: Delivering lectures may serve a training need, but it isn’t coaching.
Clarifying the difference and offering training separately keeps the coaching honest and client-led.
Dressing up lectures as coaching misrepresents what the client is actually getting.
Dismissing frameworks is unhelpful and sidesteps the client’s real request.

scenario: A client hints that they 'don't see the point in going on,' and you're unsure how serious it is.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Assume it’s just a figure of speech and continue
Gently and directly check on their safety and connect them with crisis or mental-health resources
Tell them to cheer up and look on the bright side
End the call quickly to limit your liability

explanation.best: Gently checking on safety and connecting them to resources is BEST — a possible safety concern is always taken seriously.
explanation.worst: Assuming it’s just a figure of speech is WORST because it dismisses a potential risk to the client’s life.

deeperInsight: When a client signals possible risk to their safety, coaches check directly and connect them with appropriate support.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you take a potential safety signal seriously and respond responsibly.

optionRationales.text: Brushing it off as a turn of phrase risks missing a genuine safety concern.
Checking directly and connecting them to resources responds responsibly to a possible risk.
"Cheer up" minimizes something that could be serious and offers no real support.
Hanging up to limit liability abandons the client precisely when they may need help.

scenario: A client who is in ongoing therapy for anxiety wants coaching on their career goals.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Refuse — you can’t coach anyone who is in therapy
Coach within scope on their goals, staying alert to boundaries and coordinating or referring if clinical issues arise
Take over managing their anxiety to be more efficient
Ask them to pause therapy so it doesn’t interfere with coaching

explanation.best: Coaching within scope while staying boundary-aware is BEST — coaching and therapy can run in parallel on different aims.
explanation.worst: Asking them to pause therapy is WORST because it interferes with clinical care and endangers the client.

deeperInsight: Coaching can coexist with therapy when each stays in its lane; a coach never disrupts a client’s clinical care.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you can coach appropriately alongside therapy without overstepping.

optionRationales.text: A blanket refusal is unnecessary — coaching on goals can proceed alongside therapy.
Coaching the goals while staying boundary-aware respects both roles and the client.
Taking over anxiety management steps into the therapist’s clinical role.
Telling them to pause therapy interferes with their care and could put them at risk.

scenario: A client says, 'just tell me what you'd do if you were my friend.'
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Give them friend-style advice
Warmly hold the coaching stance and explore their own wisdom rather than switching into a friend-advisor role
Say you can’t be friendly with clients at all
Give advice, but disclaim that it’s "just as a friend"

explanation.best: Holding the coaching stance while staying warm is BEST — the value is in developing their thinking, not swapping in advice.
explanation.worst: Giving friend-style advice is WORST because it abandons coaching for casual opinion.

deeperInsight: Coaching stays a professional partnership focused on the client’s own thinking, even when they invite an advice-giving role.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you hold the coaching role instead of shifting into friendly advice-giving.

optionRationales.text: Switching to friend-advice drops the coaching partnership the client is actually paying for.
Staying warm while coaching keeps the focus on drawing out their own answer.
"I can’t be friendly" misreads the request; warmth and coaching are compatible.
Advice with a "just as a friend" label is still advice, not coaching.

scenario: You've concluded a client would be better served by a therapist. How do you handle the referral?
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Abruptly tell them coaching is over and they need therapy
Share your observation with care, normalize seeking support, and offer to help them find appropriate resources
Diagnose what’s wrong so they know what to look for
Keep coaching and hope the issue resolves on its own

explanation.best: Sharing the observation with care and helping them find support is BEST — referrals are made respectfully and without diagnosis.
explanation.worst: Diagnosing what’s wrong is WORST because naming a condition is outside a coach’s scope.

deeperInsight: A good referral is warm and non-clinical: name what you notice, normalize support, and help them find the right professional.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you refer respectfully without stepping into diagnosis.

optionRationales.text: An abrupt "we’re done, go to therapy" can feel like rejection and leaves them without support.
A caring, normalizing referral with help finding resources serves the client well.
Diagnosing the client to guide their search is clinical judgment beyond coaching.
Continuing to coach and hoping it resolves ignores a need that exceeds coaching.

scenario: Despite genuine motivation, a client can’t act on anything and describes symptoms that sound clinical.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Push harder on accountability and consequences
Recognize a clinical issue may be blocking progress and explore a referral rather than more pressure
Name the specific condition you think they have
Conclude they’re simply lazy and unmotivated

explanation.best: Recognizing a possible clinical block and exploring referral is BEST — more pressure won’t fix a clinical barrier.
explanation.worst: Concluding they’re lazy is WORST because it is dismissive, judgmental, and misreads a likely clinical issue.

deeperInsight: When motivation is present but action is impossible, coaches consider a clinical barrier and refer, rather than judging or pushing.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you recognize a clinical barrier to progress and refer instead of pressuring.

optionRationales.text: Piling on accountability can’t move what may be a clinical barrier, and may add shame.
Considering a clinical block and exploring referral addresses the real obstacle.
Naming a specific condition is diagnosis, which isn’t a coach’s role.
Calling a struggling client "lazy" is judgmental and misreads a likely clinical issue.

scenario: A client asks whether they should stop taking a prescribed medication because it makes them tired.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Advise them on whether to stop the medication
Stay in scope, explore what matters to them, and direct medical questions to their prescribing clinician
Tell them to stop taking the medication
Tell them all medication is bad for you

explanation.best: Staying in scope and directing medical questions to their clinician is BEST — medication decisions are medical, not coaching.
explanation.worst: Telling them to stop the medication is WORST because advising on medication is dangerous and far outside coaching.

deeperInsight: Medical questions belong with medical professionals; coaches never advise on medication or treatment.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you keep medical decisions with the appropriate professional.

optionRationales.text: Weighing in on whether to stop is still offering medical advice.
Exploring what matters and sending medical questions to their clinician holds the boundary safely.
Telling a client to stop prescribed medication is dangerous advice well outside a coach’s scope.
"All medication is bad" is a harmful, unfounded opinion, not coaching.

scenario: A client discloses that they are currently experiencing domestic abuse at home.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Coach them on assertiveness techniques to handle it
Respond with care, recognize this exceeds coaching, and connect them with appropriate specialized support and resources
Direct them to leave their home tonight
Treat it as an ordinary coaching goal to work through

explanation.best: Responding with care and connecting them to specialized support is BEST — this is a safety matter beyond coaching.
explanation.worst: Treating it as an ordinary coaching goal is WORST because it dangerously minimizes a serious safety situation.

deeperInsight: Situations involving personal safety call for specialized resources and care, not standard coaching.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you recognize a safety situation as beyond coaching and connect the client with proper support.

optionRationales.text: Assertiveness coaching underestimates the safety dimension and could put the client at greater risk.
Care plus a warm handoff to specialized resources meets the seriousness of the situation.
Directing them to leave tonight is a high-stakes safety decision that isn’t yours to make for them.
Framing abuse as a routine coaching goal dangerously minimizes a serious safety matter.

scenario: A manager wants you to step in and mediate a live conflict between two of their team members.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Step in and mediate the dispute between the two employees yourself
Clarify that mediation is a distinct role, and either refer or contract for it separately from coaching the manager
Treat coaching the manager as if it were the same as mediating
Refuse and tell them conflict simply isn’t coachable

explanation.best: Clarifying that mediation is a separate role is BEST — coaching a manager is not the same as mediating their team.
explanation.worst: Blurring coaching the manager with mediation is WORST because it misrepresents and mixes two different services.

deeperInsight: Coaching supports the client’s own development; mediation and facilitation are distinct services that are named and contracted separately.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you distinguish coaching from facilitation/mediation.

optionRationales.text: Jumping in to mediate takes on a facilitation role distinct from coaching the manager.
Naming mediation as its own service — refer or contract separately — keeps the roles clean.
Pretending manager-coaching is mediation confuses two different services and their aims.
Conflict is very coachable for the manager; the issue is the direct-mediation ask, not coachability.

scenario: A client is sad about a recent setback but is functioning well and clearly wants to move forward.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Refer them to therapy just to be safe
Stay in the coaching role and support them — ordinary emotions don’t require a clinical referral
Diagnose them to rule anything out
Tell them to toughen up and get over it

explanation.best: Staying in the coaching role is BEST — normal sadness in a functioning client is well within coaching.
explanation.worst: Telling them to toughen up is WORST because it is dismissive and unsupportive.

deeperInsight: Not every difficult emotion needs a referral; coaches support ordinary human feeling without over-clinicalizing it.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you can tell normal emotion from a clinical concern and stay appropriately in scope.

optionRationales.text: Reflexively referring over ordinary sadness over-clinicalizes a normal human experience.
Supporting a functioning client through a setback is exactly what coaching is for.
Diagnosing "just in case" is both outside scope and unnecessary here.
"Toughen up" is dismissive and offers the client nothing.

scenario: A client says 'I'm broken, fix me' and expects you to solve their problems for them.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Position yourself as the expert who will fix them
Clarify coaching as a partnership that draws on their own capability, and reset expectations collaboratively
Agree to fix them, to keep them happy
Tell them they’re beyond help

explanation.best: Clarifying coaching as a partnership and resetting expectations is BEST — coaching builds on the client’s capability, not a fixer role.
explanation.worst: Agreeing to "fix" them is WORST because it mispositions coaching and sets up a false, dependent dynamic.

deeperInsight: Coaching treats the client as capable and resourceful; it does not cast the coach as the fixer of a "broken" person.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you hold the definition of coaching as a partnership rather than a fix-it service.

optionRationales.text: Taking the fixer role contradicts coaching’s premise that the client is whole and capable.
Resetting to a partnership that draws on their capability reframes the work honestly.
Agreeing to "fix" them entrenches a dependent, false dynamic and misrepresents coaching.
"Beyond help" is both untrue and harmful, and abandons the client.

scenario: A client mostly wants to process and understand painful childhood experiences in depth.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Do in-depth psychological work on their childhood
Acknowledge its importance, note that in-depth past processing is counseling territory, and refer while keeping coaching future-focused
Analyze their childhood to find the root cause of their issues
Tell them the past doesn’t matter, only the future

explanation.best: Acknowledging the importance and referring for past processing is BEST — deep work on the past is counseling, not coaching.
explanation.worst: Analyzing their childhood for root causes is WORST because psychological analysis is outside coaching.

deeperInsight: Coaching tends toward the present and future; in-depth exploration of the past for healing is the domain of counseling.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you distinguish coaching from counseling when a client wants deep past-focused work.

optionRationales.text: Doing in-depth childhood work steps into psychological territory beyond coaching.
Honoring its importance while referring for that work keeps coaching in its future-focused lane.
Root-cause analysis of their childhood is psychological work a coach shouldn’t perform.
Dismissing the past as irrelevant is both untrue and dismissive of what matters to them.

scenario: Anxious about a major choice, a client begs you to just make the decision for them.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Make the decision for them
Hold the coaching role — support them to weigh it and own the choice, while acknowledging the anxiety
Decide for them, but call it "guidance"
Tell them the decision is easy and they’re overthinking it

explanation.best: Supporting them to weigh and own the choice is BEST — coaching keeps decisions and their ownership with the client.
explanation.worst: Making the decision for them is WORST because it removes their autonomy, which coaching exists to strengthen.

deeperInsight: Coaching supports clients to make and own their decisions; the coach does not decide for them, however much they ask.
competencyPrinciple: Tests whether you keep decision ownership with the client rather than deciding for them.

optionRationales.text: Deciding for them strips the autonomy coaching is meant to build.
Supporting them to weigh it and own the choice honors both their autonomy and their anxiety.
Deciding for them and calling it "guidance" is the same overreach with a nicer label.
Dismissing the choice as easy ignores real anxiety and still doesn’t help them decide.

scenario: Your client has met every goal and is ready to wrap up. The well-paying sponsor hints they'd like the engagement to continue a few more months regardless.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Extend it — the sponsor is glad to keep paying
Name the client’s readiness honestly and close, or renegotiate a genuine new goal
Invent new goals to justify continuing
Quietly extend without mentioning the client is essentially done

explanation.best: Being honest about readiness and continuing only for a real goal is BEST — the client’s needs, not revenue, drive the engagement.
explanation.worst: Inventing goals to keep billing is WORST because it puts your income ahead of the client’s actual needs.

deeperInsight: Integrity means renewing or ending based on the client’s real needs, never the sponsor’s budget.

scenario: Your client mentions they've been recording your sessions and posting clips — including your words — on social media as their 'coaching journey.'
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Let it go — it’s their journey to share
Pause to discuss consent and confidentiality before it continues
Demand they delete everything or you’ll quit
Say nothing but start guarding what you say on camera

explanation.best: Pausing to discuss consent and confidentiality is BEST — recordings can expose private material and were made without agreement.
explanation.worst: Letting it go entirely is WORST because it ignores real consent and confidentiality issues in what’s shared.

deeperInsight: Client enthusiasm doesn’t override the need for clear agreements about recording and confidentiality.

scenario: You realize you've unconsciously been giving your favorite client longer sessions and faster email replies than the others who pay the same.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Keep going — they appreciate it more
Notice the imbalance and return to treating all clients equitably
Start shortchanging them to overcorrect
Quietly upsell the others to a premium tier to match

explanation.best: Noticing the imbalance and restoring equitable treatment is BEST — fairness across clients is an ethical duty.
explanation.worst: Upselling others to justify the imbalance is WORST because it monetizes unfair treatment instead of correcting it.

deeperInsight: Equitable service means each client gets what they contracted for, regardless of your personal rapport.

scenario: A prospective client offers you a generous referral fee for every new client you send to their consulting firm.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Accept — referrals are good for business
Decline any arrangement that could bias whom you refer, and keep referrals in the client’s interest
Accept but only send clients you were going to refer anyway
Accept quietly and don’t mention it to clients

explanation.best: Declining a biasing arrangement and keeping referrals client-first is BEST — referrals must serve the client, not your wallet.
explanation.worst: Taking the fee secretly is WORST because it hides a conflict that corrupts your referrals.

deeperInsight: Any incentive that could sway whom you recommend is a conflict of interest to be avoided or fully disclosed.

scenario: Your own workload has grown so heavy that you notice you're showing up tired and less present for clients.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Push through — clients don’t need to know
Acknowledge the impact on your work and adjust your load or pause taking on more
Blame the clients for being draining
Cut sessions short without telling anyone

explanation.best: Acknowledging the impact and adjusting your capacity is BEST — fitness to practice is your responsibility to protect.
explanation.worst: Silently shortening sessions is WORST because it shortchanges clients who are paying for full engagement.

deeperInsight: Ethical practice includes managing your own wellbeing so it never quietly degrades the client’s experience.

scenario: A client asks you to write a reference letter for a role, and wants you to describe leadership results the two of you both know they haven't achieved yet.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Write it as they ask — you want to support them
Offer to write honestly about what you’ve genuinely observed
Embellish just enough to be believable
Refuse and lecture them about honesty

explanation.best: Writing honestly about what you’ve actually observed is BEST — a reference must be truthful.
explanation.worst: Embellishing to be believable is WORST because it’s a deliberate misrepresentation with your name on it.

deeperInsight: Supporting a client never extends to vouching for accomplishments that aren’t real.

scenario: Your laptop, which holds session notes, is stolen. The notes include identifiable client details.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Say nothing and hope for the best
Inform affected clients promptly and take steps to secure their data going forward
Tell only the clients who ask
Downplay it if a client happens to mention a concern

explanation.best: Promptly informing affected clients and improving safeguards is BEST — clients have a right to know their data was exposed.
explanation.worst: Saying nothing is WORST because it hides a breach of the confidentiality they trusted you with.

deeperInsight: A data breach triggers a duty of transparency and remediation, not silence.

scenario: In a group coaching program, one participant privately asks you how another specific participant is progressing.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Share a quick update — they’re in the same group
Decline and keep each participant’s progress confidential
Share only positive things about the other person
Hint at it without naming specifics

explanation.best: Declining and protecting each participant’s confidentiality is BEST — group membership doesn’t waive individual privacy.
explanation.worst: Sharing an update is WORST because it breaches the other participant’s confidentiality.

deeperInsight: In group settings, each person’s information stays theirs unless they’ve agreed otherwise.

scenario: A client wants to prepay for a year of coaching in cash, in several under-the-radar installments, and asks you not to invoice.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Agree — a paying client is a paying client
Decline the irregular arrangement and keep transparent, properly documented billing
Accept but keep your own private record just in case
Accept and avoid asking why

explanation.best: Keeping transparent, documented billing is BEST — irregular, undocumented payments are an ethical and legal red flag.
explanation.worst: Accepting while avoiding the question is WORST because it willfully ignores a possible attempt to hide something.

deeperInsight: Sound financial practices protect both you and the client and keep the relationship above board.

scenario: You're asked to coach the spouse of a current client. The two clients' goals would inevitably touch on each other.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Take it on — more business is good
Name the confidentiality and conflict risks, and decline or set clear boundaries
Take it and simply avoid mentioning either to the other
Take it and use what you learn from one to help the other

explanation.best: Naming the risks and declining or setting firm boundaries is BEST — overlapping intimate relationships threaten confidentiality and neutrality.
explanation.worst: Using what you learn from one to help the other is WORST because it’s a direct confidentiality breach.

deeperInsight: Closely connected clients create conflicts that must be surfaced and managed, not quietly navigated.

scenario: A client gives you a glowing testimonial you feature on your site. Months later they email asking you to take it down.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Leave it up — they already consented once
Remove it promptly as requested
Remove their name but keep the quote
Ask them to reconsider before you’ll take it down

explanation.best: Removing it promptly is BEST — consent can be withdrawn, and their wishes about their own words govern.
explanation.worst: Keeping the quote after stripping the name is WORST because it defies a clear withdrawal of consent.

deeperInsight: Consent to use a client’s words is ongoing and revocable, not a one-time permanent release.

scenario: A client asks you to coach them toward a plan that, as they describe it, would clearly harm their team to benefit only themselves.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Coach the plan neutrally — it’s their choice
Stay curious and surface the impact on others without imposing your judgment
Refuse and tell them the plan is wrong
Secretly steer them away from it

explanation.best: Staying curious and surfacing the impact while respecting their autonomy is BEST — you raise awareness without moralizing or manipulating.
explanation.worst: Secretly steering them away is WORST because it manipulates the client under the guise of coaching.

deeperInsight: You can invite reflection on consequences to others without either endorsing harm or covertly controlling the client.

scenario: You discover a peer is marketing themselves using your client testimonials, lightly reworded, as if they were their own.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Ignore it — testimonials get copied
Address it with the peer directly and, if needed, through proper channels
Copy some of their material in return
Post a public callout naming and shaming them

explanation.best: Addressing it directly and escalating properly is BEST — misappropriated client material is a real integrity issue handled professionally.
explanation.worst: Copying their material in return is WORST because it answers one violation by committing another.

deeperInsight: Integrity means responding to a breach through legitimate channels, not retaliation.

scenario: Partway through an engagement, a client asks whether the assessment tool you use is one you're actually certified in — and you're not.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Assure them you are — you know it well enough
Be honest about your certification status and offer options
Change the subject
Imply you are without saying so directly

explanation.best: Being honest about your certification status is BEST — clients deserve accurate information about your qualifications.
explanation.worst: Falsely assuring them is WORST because it misrepresents your competence to keep their confidence.

deeperInsight: Honesty about credentials and tools is non-negotiable, even mid-engagement.

scenario: A client casually reveals plans to commit what sounds like significant financial fraud at their company.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Keep coaching the underlying stress and stay out of it
Acknowledge the seriousness, clarify confidentiality’s limits, and don’t assist or endorse it
Help them think through how to do it more cleverly
End the session and never explain why

explanation.best: Acknowledging the seriousness and clarifying the limits of confidentiality is BEST — you neither assist nor pretend it wasn’t said.
explanation.worst: Helping them do it more cleverly is WORST because it makes you complicit in the wrongdoing.

deeperInsight: Confidentiality has limits, and a coach never facilitates a client’s unlawful or unethical plan.

scenario: A client wants intensive weight and fitness coaching. In passing, they mention a history of a serious eating disorder.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Proceed with aggressive fitness and diet goals
Recognize the risk, and coach only within scope while encouraging appropriate specialized support
Tell them they shouldn’t focus on their body at all
Design a strict meal and exercise plan for them

explanation.best: Coaching within scope while encouraging specialized support is BEST — an eating-disorder history can make aggressive body goals unsafe.
explanation.worst: Designing a strict meal-and-exercise plan is WORST because it’s both outside coaching and potentially harmful given the history.

deeperInsight: A relevant clinical history changes what’s safe to coach and when specialized help belongs in the picture.

scenario: Your client wants you to act as their accountability 'boss' — checking their to-do list daily and pushing them when they slack.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Take on the daily task-master role they’re asking for
Clarify what coaching is and co-design accountability they own, rather than becoming their manager
Refuse and tell them accountability isn’t coaching
Agree, then quietly stop after a week

explanation.best: Clarifying coaching and co-designing ownership-based accountability is BEST — coaching builds self-direction, not a boss relationship.
explanation.worst: Agreeing then quietly quitting the role is WORST because it sets a false expectation and then abandons it.

deeperInsight: Accountability in coaching is designed with the client to strengthen ownership, not imposed like management.

scenario: A client asks you to attend their performance review to advocate for them and speak to their growth.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Agree to attend and advocate on their behalf
Clarify that advocacy isn’t the coaching role, and coach them to prepare and represent themselves
Refuse flatly with no discussion
Attend but stay silent the whole time

explanation.best: Coaching them to prepare and represent themselves is BEST — advocacy would step outside the coaching role.
explanation.worst: Attending to advocate for them is WORST because it turns you into their representative rather than their coach.

deeperInsight: Coaching builds the client’s own capacity to show up; it doesn’t speak for them.

scenario: A client keeps seeking deep, cathartic emotional release each session, treating it like the point of the work rather than a step in it.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Provide the cathartic sessions they want each time
Acknowledge the emotion, and name that ongoing catharsis may be better served by counseling
Tell them to stop being so emotional
Ignore it and stick rigidly to goals

explanation.best: Acknowledging the emotion while naming a possible counseling need is BEST — repeated catharsis as the goal points beyond coaching.
explanation.worst: Telling them to stop being emotional is WORST because it shames the client and damages safety.

deeperInsight: Emotion has a place in coaching, but ongoing emotional processing as the aim is counseling territory.

scenario: A client wants your help making a big investment decision and asks which specific funds they should put their savings into.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Recommend specific funds you like
Explore what matters to them and refer specific investment advice to a licensed financial professional
Tell them investing is too risky to bother
Walk them through exactly how to allocate the money

explanation.best: Exploring their priorities and referring specifics to a licensed professional is BEST — investment advice is outside coaching.
explanation.worst: Walking them through a specific allocation is WORST because it’s regulated financial advice, not coaching.

deeperInsight: Coaching clarifies what matters; specific financial, legal, or medical direction belongs to licensed experts.

scenario: Your client seems unusually elevated — talking rapidly, sleeping little, and making a string of impulsive, high-risk commitments.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Match their energy and help them act fast
Express care, and gently encourage them to check in with a health professional
Diagnose what you think is going on
Ignore it as just enthusiasm

explanation.best: Expressing care and encouraging a professional check-in is BEST — these signs may be clinical and warrant expert attention.
explanation.worst: Offering a diagnosis is WORST because naming a condition is outside a coach’s competence.

deeperInsight: Coaches notice possible clinical signs and encourage appropriate help without diagnosing.

scenario: A client wants you to help them make sense of their faith and what God wants for their life.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Offer your own spiritual guidance and beliefs
Coach around what meaning and values they’re seeking, and suggest a spiritual advisor for doctrine
Tell them faith has no place in coaching
Take on the role of their spiritual director

explanation.best: Coaching around their meaning and values while referring doctrine elsewhere is BEST — spiritual direction is a distinct role.
explanation.worst: Becoming their spiritual director is WORST because it takes on a role well outside coaching.

deeperInsight: Coaching can explore what matters to a client without becoming religious or spiritual counsel.

scenario: A client expects you to be reachable any time day or night for 'emergencies,' and gets upset when you're not.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Agree to be on call around the clock
Clarify coaching’s scope and hours, and point to real crisis resources for emergencies
Tell them to stop being needy
Vaguely promise availability you can’t sustain

explanation.best: Clarifying scope and pointing to crisis resources is BEST — coaching isn’t crisis support, and clear boundaries protect both of you.
explanation.worst: Vaguely promising availability you can’t sustain is WORST because it sets up broken expectations and possible harm in a real crisis.

deeperInsight: Coaching operates within defined boundaries; genuine emergencies need dedicated crisis services.

scenario: A leader you're coaching frames their 'problem' as one difficult employee — but it's clearly a systemic HR and policy issue.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Coach them to just manage the one employee
Coach the leader while noting that parts of this may need HR or organizational channels
Tell them to file an HR complaint immediately
Take on investigating the situation yourself

explanation.best: Coaching the leader while flagging the HR/organizational channels is BEST — some of this sits outside what coaching resolves.
explanation.worst: Investigating the situation yourself is WORST because it steps into an HR/organizational role that isn’t coaching.

deeperInsight: Coaching develops the leader; systemic and HR matters route to the functions built for them.

scenario: A client wants you to give them your professional network and open doors to specific people you know.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Start making introductions on their behalf
Clarify that door-opening is a mentoring/networking role, and coach them to build their own approach
Refuse and say your network is private
Promise introductions you don’t intend to make

explanation.best: Clarifying the role and coaching them to build their own approach is BEST — leveraging your network is mentoring, not coaching.
explanation.worst: Promising introductions you won’t make is WORST because it’s a dishonest way to avoid the boundary.

deeperInsight: Coaching grows the client’s own capability; brokering access is a different relationship entirely.

scenario: A client discloses they've been having thoughts of self-harm, though they say they're 'probably fine.'
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Take the reassurance at face value and continue
Take it seriously, check on their safety, and connect them with crisis/mental-health support
Tell them everyone feels that way sometimes
Quickly wrap up the session to step back

explanation.best: Taking it seriously and connecting them with support is BEST — possible self-harm is always handled with care, not assumption.
explanation.worst: Taking the reassurance at face value is WORST because it risks missing a genuine danger to the client.

deeperInsight: When self-harm is mentioned, safety and appropriate professional support come before anything else.

scenario: A client wants you to mediate the ongoing conflict in their marriage and 'help them both communicate better.'
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Take on the couples mediation they’re asking for
Clarify that couples work is outside coaching, and refer them to a couples therapist
Tell them to just work it out themselves
Coach one partner on how to change the other

explanation.best: Clarifying scope and referring to a couples therapist is BEST — relationship mediation is a distinct clinical service.
explanation.worst: Taking on the couples mediation is WORST because it’s well outside a coach’s role and competence.

deeperInsight: Coaching supports an individual’s own growth; mediating a relationship is a different profession.

scenario: A client asks you, as their coach, to also become their business partner in a venture they're excited about.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Say yes — you believe in the venture
Recognize the dual-role conflict and keep the coaching relationship separate from any business tie
Invest quietly without telling them
Agree but keep coaching them about the same venture

explanation.best: Keeping coaching separate from any business partnership is BEST — becoming a stakeholder destroys coaching neutrality.
explanation.worst: Continuing to coach them about the very venture you’re partnered in is WORST because your stake corrupts the coaching.

deeperInsight: A financial stake in the client’s decisions is a dual relationship that coaching can’t survive intact.

scenario: A client keeps asking you to just do parts of the work for them — draft the email, write the plan — because you'd 'do it better.'
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Do the tasks for them to be helpful
Keep the work theirs and coach them through producing it
Refuse and tell them to figure it out alone
Do it once, then resent it and stop

explanation.best: Keeping the work theirs while coaching them through it is BEST — coaching builds their capability rather than substituting for it.
explanation.worst: Doing the tasks for them is WORST because it makes you their assistant and undercuts their growth.

deeperInsight: Coaching develops the client’s own capacity; doing the work for them creates dependence.

scenario: A client is clearly grieving a recent loss and asks you to 'just help me get through the sadness.'
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Take on helping them process the grief itself
Acknowledge the grief, and recognize that grief support may be counseling while coaching what’s in scope
Tell them to focus on the future instead
Avoid the topic and steer to goals

explanation.best: Acknowledging the grief and recognizing possible counseling needs is BEST — processing grief itself can exceed coaching.
explanation.worst: Telling them to just focus on the future is WORST because it dismisses their grief and offers no real support.

deeperInsight: Coaches meet grief with care and know when processing it belongs with a counselor.

scenario: You catch yourself already 'knowing' where the session should go before the client has even finished describing their situation.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Steer toward the conclusion you’ve already reached
Set your assumption aside and stay genuinely open to where the client leads
Ask questions designed to confirm your hunch
Keep the conclusion to yourself but quietly aim for it

explanation.best: Setting the assumption aside and staying open is BEST — a coaching mindset holds conclusions lightly.
explanation.worst: Steering toward your pre-formed conclusion is WORST because it imposes your map over the client’s reality.

deeperInsight: A coaching mindset means noticing your certainty and choosing curiosity over it.

scenario: A session goes badly and you leave feeling you failed the client. The feeling lingers into your next few sessions.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Ignore it and power through
Reflect on it, and seek supervision or feedback to learn from it
Decide you’re not cut out for coaching
Blame the client for the bad session

explanation.best: Reflecting and seeking supervision is BEST — a coaching mindset grows through ongoing self-examination.
explanation.worst: Blaming the client is WORST because it avoids the reflection that would actually help you develop.

deeperInsight: Difficult sessions are material for growth when met with reflection rather than defensiveness.

scenario: Your client makes a choice you're confident is a mistake, but it's genuinely their choice to make.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Tell them plainly they’re making a mistake
Trust their autonomy and explore their thinking and what they’ll watch for
Withhold support to signal disapproval
Pretend to agree while hoping they fail

explanation.best: Trusting their autonomy while exploring their thinking is BEST — a coaching mindset respects the client as the decision-maker.
explanation.worst: Secretly hoping they fail is WORST because it abandons the client’s interest for your ego.

deeperInsight: Respecting client autonomy means supporting their right to choose, even when you’d choose differently.

scenario: Fifteen minutes into the session your client has drifted across four different topics with real energy but no clear focus.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Follow whichever topic seems most interesting to you
Pause to partner with them on which single focus would make this session valuable
Let them keep wandering to honor their process
Pick the topic you think matters most and run with it

explanation.best: Partnering on a single valuable focus is BEST — the session agreement is co-created, keeping the work purposeful.
explanation.worst: Picking the topic yourself is WORST because it takes over a choice that belongs to the client.

deeperInsight: A clear session focus, agreed together, turns scattered energy into progress.

scenario: Your client sets today's goal, but by mid-session it's clear the real issue underneath is different and more important to them.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Stick to the original goal you both agreed on
Name what you’re noticing and check whether to shift the focus
Switch silently to the deeper issue
Tell them they picked the wrong goal

explanation.best: Naming the shift and checking whether to refocus is BEST — agreements are maintained and adjusted openly.
explanation.worst: Telling them they picked the wrong goal is WORST because it’s a judgment that ignores co-creation.

deeperInsight: A session agreement is a living understanding, revisited together when the real work surfaces.

scenario: A new client is vague about what success would look like: 'I just want things to be better.'
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Start coaching and hope it becomes clear
Partner to define what "better" looks like and how they’ll know
Assign them a specific goal to make it concrete
Tell them they need to come back when they know

explanation.best: Defining what "better" looks like and how they’ll know is BEST — it turns a vague wish into a workable agreement.
explanation.worst: Assigning them a goal is WORST because it substitutes your definition of success for theirs.

deeperInsight: Clear measures of success, co-created, make coaching purposeful and progress visible.

scenario: A client hesitates, then says, 'I'm worried this will sound stupid, but...' and trails off, watching you.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Reassure them fast and rush them to continue
Warmly signal there’s no judgment here and give them space to go on
Tell them nothing they say could be stupid, then move on
Fill the pause with a question of your own

explanation.best: Signaling safety and giving them space is BEST — trust deepens when hesitation is met with patience.
explanation.worst: Filling the pause with your own question is WORST because it takes the floor just as they were about to risk something.

deeperInsight: Safety is built in the small moments where a client tests whether it’s okay to be honest.

scenario: Your client, from a culture different from yours, describes a family obligation you find limiting — but it clearly matters deeply to them.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Gently suggest they prioritize their own goals over it
Respect its importance and coach within their values and context
Point out how it’s holding them back
Avoid the topic since you don’t relate to it

explanation.best: Respecting its importance and coaching within their context is BEST — trust rests on honoring the client’s values and identity.
explanation.worst: Suggesting they deprioritize it is WORST because it imposes your values over theirs.

deeperInsight: Cultural and personal values are the frame for the client’s work, not obstacles to be corrected.

scenario: Midway through, your client says quietly, 'Honestly, I'm not sure this coaching is even working for me.'
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Defend the value of coaching and your approach
Welcome the honesty and explore what they need that they’re not getting
Take it personally and get quiet
Reassure them it’s working and move on

explanation.best: Welcoming the honesty and exploring their needs is BEST — inviting hard feedback deepens trust and improves the work.
explanation.worst: Defending yourself is WORST because it makes it unsafe for the client to be candid again.

deeperInsight: A client’s doubt is a gift when met with openness rather than defensiveness.

scenario: Your mind keeps drifting to your own stressful afternoon while the client is speaking about something clearly important to them.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Keep half-listening and nod along
Notice the drift, let your own concerns go for now, and return fully to the client
Interrupt to ask them to summarize
Push your worry down and grip harder to your planned questions

explanation.best: Noticing the drift and returning fully to the client is BEST — presence is the ongoing choice to come back.
explanation.worst: Half-listening and nodding is WORST because the client can feel the absence and it undermines the work.

deeperInsight: Presence isn’t never getting distracted; it’s noticing and returning, again and again.

scenario: The client shares something heavy and the room goes still. You feel a strong urge to say something comforting to ease the discomfort.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Jump in with reassurance to lift the mood
Stay present with them in the moment without rushing to fix the feeling
Change to a lighter topic
Share a similar experience of your own

explanation.best: Staying present without rushing to fix is BEST — presence lets the client have their own experience.
explanation.worst: Jumping in with reassurance is WORST because it serves your discomfort, not the client’s process.

deeperInsight: Sometimes the most present thing a coach can do is stay, and say nothing.

scenario: You don't know what to ask next. A silence opens up and you feel the pressure to sound insightful.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Ask a clever-sounding question to fill the gap
Stay comfortable in the not-knowing and let a genuine question emerge
Admit you’re stuck and suggest wrapping up
Default to a generic question you always use

explanation.best: Staying comfortable in not-knowing is BEST — presence includes trusting the space rather than performing insight.
explanation.worst: Admitting you’re stuck and suggesting you wrap up is WORST because it abandons the moment to escape discomfort.

deeperInsight: Not-knowing, held with presence, often produces the most honest and useful next question.

scenario: Your client describes a 'small annoyance' at work, but their voice tightens and they've now mentioned it three times.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Take them at their word that it’s small
Reflect that it seems to carry more weight than "small," and invite them to explore it
Tell them it’s obviously a big deal
Move on to the topic they said they wanted

explanation.best: Reflecting the gap and inviting exploration is BEST — active listening notices what repetition and tone reveal.
explanation.worst: Telling them it’s obviously a big deal is WORST because it overrides their framing with your conclusion.

deeperInsight: How often and how intensely something is mentioned often says more than the label the client gives it.

scenario: The client pauses and says, 'well, everyone says I should be grateful,' then moves quickly on.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Follow them to the next thing
Gently reflect the "should" and offer them the choice to look at it
Tell them they shouldn’t care what everyone says
Ask a rapid series of questions about who "everyone" is

explanation.best: Reflecting the "should" and offering the choice is BEST — active listening catches the loaded phrase left behind.
explanation.worst: Firing off rapid questions is WORST because it interrogates rather than listens.

deeperInsight: Small, charged phrases the client hurries past are often doorways worth gently naming.

scenario: After the client speaks for a few minutes, you want to be sure you've truly understood what matters to them.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Assume you got it and keep moving
Reflect back the essence, including the feeling, and check it with them
Repeat their words back exactly
Summarize it as what you would have meant

explanation.best: Reflecting the essence and feeling, then checking, is BEST — it confirms understanding and helps the client feel heard.
explanation.worst: Summarizing it as what you would have meant is WORST because it replaces their meaning with yours.

deeperInsight: Good reflection captures the client’s meaning and emotion, not just their words or your interpretation.

scenario: Your client keeps describing what everyone else in their life wants, but never what they want.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Suggest what you think they want
Gently reflect the pattern and invite them to notice whose voice is missing
Tell them to stop worrying about others
List the options they should consider

explanation.best: Reflecting the pattern and inviting them to notice is BEST — it evokes awareness without handing them the answer.
explanation.worst: Suggesting what they want is WORST because it fills in the very awareness they need to reach themselves.

deeperInsight: Naming a pattern and offering it back opens awareness the client can then own.

scenario: A client is stuck describing a problem in the same looping way for the third time.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Offer your analysis of the loop
Invite a shift in perspective — "if a mentor you admire saw this, what might they notice?"
Tell them they’re going in circles
Move on to a different problem

explanation.best: Inviting a perspective shift is BEST — a fresh vantage point evokes awareness that the loop is hiding.
explanation.worst: Moving on to a different problem is WORST because it abandons the stuck spot instead of opening it.

deeperInsight: When a client loops, a new perspective often reveals what more of the same questioning can’t.

scenario: Your client has a realization and says, 'huh, I never saw it that way,' then goes quiet.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Quickly move to the next question
Give the insight room and invite them to explore what it opens up
Explain why the insight is significant
Congratulate them and move to action

explanation.best: Giving the insight room and inviting exploration is BEST — awareness deepens when it’s allowed to unfold.
explanation.worst: Explaining why it’s significant is WORST because it takes over the meaning-making that’s theirs to do.

deeperInsight: A fresh insight is a threshold; lingering there lets the client discover what it makes possible.

scenario: Your client has a strong insight but ends the session with no sense of what they'll actually do differently.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Assign them a concrete next step
Invite them to design a next step that follows from the insight
Give them a menu of options to choose from
Leave it, since the insight is enough

explanation.best: Inviting them to design their own next step is BEST — clients act on and sustain what they create.
explanation.worst: Assigning the step yourself is WORST because it takes ownership of the action away from the client.

deeperInsight: Growth happens when awareness is translated into action the client designs and owns.

scenario: Your client committed to an action last week and did it — and mentions it in one flat sentence before rushing on.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Note it and move to the next thing
Pause to help them recognize what worked and what it tells them about themselves
Praise them briefly, then move on
Immediately raise the bar with a bigger goal

explanation.best: Pausing to help them recognize what worked is BEST — integrating a win builds momentum and self-belief.
explanation.worst: Noting it and moving on is WORST because it skips the reflection that turns a small win into lasting growth.

deeperInsight: Progress compounds when the client harvests what worked, not just when they set the next target.

scenario: A client asks you to date an invoice to last year so they can claim the expense on taxes that have already closed.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Backdate it — it’s a minor courtesy
Decline, and provide a correctly dated invoice
Backdate it but keep the true date in your own records
Backdate it and ask them to keep it between you

explanation.best: Providing a correctly dated invoice is BEST — falsifying financial records isn’t a favor you can ethically do.
explanation.worst: Backdating and asking them to keep it quiet is WORST because the secrecy confirms you both know it’s fraud.

deeperInsight: Honest records protect you and the client; a "small" falsification is still a falsification.

scenario: You receive a legal request compelling you to hand over your notes about a client involved in a lawsuit.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Refuse outright to protect confidentiality
Seek legal advice, comply only as legally required, and inform the client where possible
Hand over everything immediately to avoid trouble
Quietly destroy the notes

explanation.best: Getting legal advice, complying only as required, and informing the client is BEST — confidentiality yields to law, handled carefully.
explanation.worst: Destroying the notes is WORST because it’s obstruction and a serious ethical and legal breach.

deeperInsight: When law and confidentiality collide you follow the law thoughtfully — never by hiding or destroying records.

scenario: About to co-lead a program, you learn your co-facilitator has been telling clients they hold an ICF credential they don’t actually have.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Say nothing — it’s their claim, not yours
Address it directly and refuse to let the misrepresentation stand in your shared program
Mirror the vagueness to keep things smooth
Report them publicly online before anything else

explanation.best: Addressing it and refusing to let the false claim stand is BEST — you can’t knowingly host a misrepresentation.
explanation.worst: Saying nothing is WORST because letting the false credential stand in your program makes you complicit.

deeperInsight: Integrity includes not lending your name to someone else’s misrepresentation.

scenario: In a session, a client mentions non-public news that their company is about to be acquired — information you could easily profit from.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Act on it quietly; they volunteered it
Don’t use the information, and keep it confidential
Use it just a little, to be safe
Pass it to a friend so it’s not technically you

explanation.best: Not using the information and keeping it confidential is BEST — client disclosures are never yours to profit from.
explanation.worst: Acting on it is WORST because it’s a betrayal of trust and almost certainly illegal.

deeperInsight: Confidential information exists to serve the client, never the coach’s advantage.

scenario: The sponsor paying for the coaching asks you to share your notes so they can build a case to terminate your client.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Share them — the sponsor is the paying party
Decline, and hold to the confidentiality terms everyone agreed
Share a "summary" that leans negative
Warn the client to quit before they’re fired

explanation.best: Declining and holding the agreed confidentiality is BEST — coaching notes can’t be turned into evidence against the client.
explanation.worst: Handing over the notes is WORST because it betrays the client and weaponizes the coaching relationship.

deeperInsight: A sponsor funds coaching; they don’t get to convert it into a case against the person being coached.

scenario: A client asks you to delete your notes from a session where they disclosed a safety concern involving someone else.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Delete them as asked
Explain why some records must be kept, and handle them per your policy and any duty of care
Delete them but quietly keep a screenshot
Delete them and put it out of your mind

explanation.best: Explaining retention and handling it per policy and duty of care is BEST — safeguarding records aren’t simply deletable on request.
explanation.worst: Deleting them and putting it out of mind is WORST because it abandons a possible duty of care around a safety concern.

deeperInsight: Some records carry a duty of care that overrides a routine deletion request.

scenario: During a session your client’s speech becomes disorganized and they describe beliefs disconnected from reality, appearing frightened.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Coach them through the beliefs as if they were goals
Prioritize their safety and help them connect with urgent mental-health support
Tell them their beliefs aren’t real
End the call abruptly

explanation.best: Prioritizing safety and connecting them with urgent support is BEST — an acute mental-health episode is far outside coaching.
explanation.worst: Coaching the disorganized beliefs as if they were goals is WORST because it’s unsafe and well beyond a coach’s role.

deeperInsight: When someone appears to be in acute crisis, safety and professional help come before anything resembling coaching.

scenario: A client asks you to write large parts of their book for them, since you’re "good with words," as part of your coaching.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Start ghostwriting the chapters for them
Clarify that writing it isn’t coaching, and coach them to write it (or refer to a ghostwriter)
Write a little to get them started
Take it on as a separate paid writing gig without discussing the role change

explanation.best: Clarifying the boundary and coaching them to write it is BEST — producing the work for them isn’t coaching.
explanation.worst: Ghostwriting the chapters is WORST because it makes you the author and abandons the coaching role entirely.

deeperInsight: Coaching builds the client’s own capacity to create; doing the creating for them is a different service.

scenario: A client struggling with their teenager asks you to talk to the teen directly and "straighten them out."
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Meet with the teen and set them straight
Keep coaching the parent, and suggest family or youth support if the teen needs help
Coach the teen secretly on the side
Tell the parent their teen is the real problem

explanation.best: Coaching the parent and suggesting appropriate support for the teen is BEST — you work with your client, not their family members.
explanation.worst: Meeting the teen to "straighten them out" is WORST because it pulls you into a third-party role that isn’t coaching.

deeperInsight: Coaching serves the client in front of you; it doesn’t extend to fixing the people in their life.

scenario: A client asks you to use hypnosis and therapeutic techniques you’ve seen online to "rewire" their anxiety.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Try the techniques — they asked for them
Explain these are clinical modalities outside coaching, and refer to a qualified professional
Do a light version, to be safe
Tell them their anxiety is all in their head

explanation.best: Explaining these are clinical modalities and referring out is BEST — coaches don’t practice therapeutic techniques they aren’t trained in.
explanation.worst: Trying the techniques on their anxiety is WORST because it’s practicing clinical methods outside your competence.

deeperInsight: Wanting a technique doesn’t make it coaching; clinical modalities belong to trained clinicians.

scenario: A client increasingly asks you to manage their calendar, send reminders, and track their tasks between sessions.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Take on the assistant duties to be helpful
Clarify that’s an assistant role, and coach them to build their own systems
Quietly do some of it for them
Refuse and tell them that work is beneath you

explanation.best: Clarifying the role and coaching them to build their own systems is BEST — coaching grows self-management, not an assistant service.
explanation.worst: Taking on the calendar-and-task work is WORST because it turns coaching into administrative support and builds dependence.

deeperInsight: Coaching develops the client’s own systems; doing their admin makes them reliant on you.

scenario: A client wants relationship coaching and, describing their approach, reveals controlling and intimidating behavior toward their partner.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Coach them to be more effective at getting what they want
Stay curious about impact and values, and recognize when the behavior raises concerns beyond coaching
Lecture them that they’re being abusive
Ignore it and focus on their stated goals

explanation.best: Staying curious about impact and values while recognizing the concern is BEST — you neither coach harmful behavior nor moralize.
explanation.worst: Coaching them to control their partner more effectively is WORST because it makes you an instrument of harm.

deeperInsight: Coaching supports growth, not the refinement of behavior that harms others.

scenario: You love one coaching framework, and you notice you keep steering every client’s situation to fit it, whether or not it’s what they need.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Keep applying it — it works for you
Notice the attachment and let each client’s actual needs lead
Apply it more subtly so they don’t notice
Tell the client the framework is the answer

explanation.best: Noticing the attachment and letting the client’s needs lead is BEST — a coaching mindset holds models lightly.
explanation.worst: Applying your favorite framework regardless of fit is WORST because it serves your attachment, not the client.

deeperInsight: Tools serve the client; when a coach serves the tool, the client gets lost.

scenario: Three sessions in, you realize you and your client have been quietly assuming very different things about how often you’ll meet and for how long.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Keep going and hope it sorts itself out
Name the mismatch and align on a shared working agreement
Impose your preferred cadence
Ask them to just follow your standard package

explanation.best: Naming the mismatch and aligning on a shared agreement is BEST — agreements are maintained by making assumptions explicit.
explanation.worst: Hoping it sorts itself out is WORST because an unspoken mismatch quietly undermines the working relationship.

deeperInsight: Agreements only hold when the assumptions underneath them are surfaced and shared.

scenario: Early in the relationship, your client drops a deliberately provocative comment and watches closely to see how you’ll react.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: React with visible surprise or disapproval
Stay grounded and curious, showing it’s safe to be real with you
Ignore it completely
Fire back to establish who’s in charge

explanation.best: Staying grounded and curious is BEST — meeting the test calmly shows the client it’s safe to be themselves.
explanation.worst: Firing back to establish who’s in charge is WORST because it turns a trust test into a power struggle.

deeperInsight: A provocative comment is often a test of safety; how you hold it sets the tone for the whole relationship.

scenario: Mid-session, your phone buzzes with what you can see is an urgent personal message, and you feel the pull to check it.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Glance at it quickly while the client keeps talking
Leave it, stay fully with the client, and deal with it afterward
Interrupt to say you need to check something
Speed the client along so you can get to your phone

explanation.best: Leaving it and staying fully present is BEST — presence means the client has your whole attention for their time.
explanation.worst: Glancing at the message mid-session is WORST because divided attention breaks the presence the client is paying for.

deeperInsight: Presence is a commitment to be fully here; even a quick glance signals the client is competing for your attention.

scenario: Within a few minutes, your client says they’re "totally over" a situation and then describes it with obvious lingering emotion.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Accept the first statement and move on
Gently reflect the two things you’re hearing and let them explore
Point out that they’re contradicting themselves
Decide for them which version is true

explanation.best: Reflecting the two things you’re hearing is BEST — active listening surfaces the contradiction for the client to explore.
explanation.worst: Deciding for them which version is true is WORST because it replaces their exploration with your conclusion.

deeperInsight: A contradiction is a doorway; naming it gently lets the client discover what’s really there.

scenario: Your client stops and asks, "okay, what do you think I’m supposed to realize here?"
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Tell them the realization you have in mind
Turn it back with curiosity about what they’re noticing
Say there’s no realization to be had
Drop a hint and let them guess it

explanation.best: Turning it back to what they’re noticing is BEST — awareness has to be theirs, not handed to them.
explanation.worst: Telling them the realization you have in mind is WORST because it hands over the insight instead of evoking it.

deeperInsight: When a client fishes for your answer, the gift is handing the question back, not the answer.

scenario: Energized, your client wants to commit to ten new goals this session and leave with a plan for all of them.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Help them build plans for all ten
Explore what matters most and help them choose where to start
Tell them ten is far too many
Pick the goals for them

explanation.best: Exploring what matters most and choosing a starting point is BEST — growth comes from focused, owned action, not scattered plans.
explanation.worst: Picking the goals for them is WORST because it takes ownership away from the client.

deeperInsight: Ten goals at once usually means none; helping the client focus turns energy into progress.

scenario: Your client hit a meaningful goal but waves it off: "that was just luck, anyone could have done it."
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Agree and move on to the next goal
Help them examine what they actually did to make it happen
Insist that they should feel proud
Let the self-dismissal pass unremarked

explanation.best: Helping them examine what they actually did is BEST — owning their agency in a win builds the confidence that fuels growth.
explanation.worst: Agreeing it was just luck is WORST because it reinforces the self-dismissal and erases their role in the success.

deeperInsight: Growth compounds when clients can see and own their part in what worked.

scenario: To save time, you’ve started pasting your session notes — including client names and details — into an AI tool to auto-summarize them.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Keep doing it — it’s a big time-saver
Stop, and only use tools with clear consent and proper data protection for client information
Remove just the names but keep the rest
Ask the AI tool not to store anything, and continue

explanation.best: Only using tools with consent and proper data protection is BEST — client information can’t go into third-party tools without safeguards.
explanation.worst: Continuing because it’s convenient is WORST because it exposes confidential client data without consent.

deeperInsight: New tools don’t change the rule: confidential client data needs consent and protection before it goes anywhere.

scenario: You already coach a manager. Their direct report now asks you to coach them too — and neither knows about the other.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Take both quietly; you can keep them separate
Address the confidentiality and conflict risks with both before deciding whether to proceed
Take both and use context from each to help the other
Coach the report, but mention it to the manager

explanation.best: Addressing the confidentiality and conflict risks with both is BEST — overlapping reporting lines need transparency, not silent management.
explanation.worst: Using context from one to help the other is WORST because it breaches confidentiality across the reporting line.

deeperInsight: Coaching people in the same chain of command demands disclosure and airtight boundaries.

scenario: You realize a scheduling error on your part caused your client to miss a session right before an important deadline.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Downplay it and hope they don’t notice
Own the error honestly, apologize, and make it right
Blame it on a calendar glitch
Quietly offer a discount without acknowledging what happened

explanation.best: Owning the error and making it right is BEST — integrity means taking responsibility for your mistakes.
explanation.worst: Blaming a calendar glitch is WORST because it dodges responsibility with a false excuse.

deeperInsight: Trust survives honest mistakes; it rarely survives the cover-up.

scenario: A cash-strapped startup client offers you equity and free use of their product instead of your fee.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Accept — it could be worth a lot someday
Weigh how a financial stake could bias your coaching, and decline or set clear boundaries
Accept the equity but keep it to yourself
Accept, and start steering them toward decisions that raise the equity’s value

explanation.best: Weighing the bias and setting boundaries is BEST — a stake in the client’s outcomes can quietly compromise your neutrality.
explanation.worst: Steering them toward decisions that raise your equity’s value is WORST because it turns coaching into self-dealing.

deeperInsight: Any financial stake in a client’s decisions is a conflict to handle deliberately, not embrace casually.

scenario: A client had a breakthrough you’d love to feature as a case study in a paid course you’re launching.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Use it — it’s a great story and you’ll change the details
Get explicit consent for exactly how their story is used, protecting confidentiality
Use it anonymized without asking
Use it and offer them a free course seat as thanks

explanation.best: Getting explicit consent for exactly how it’s used is BEST — a client’s story is theirs, even with details changed.
explanation.worst: Using it because you changed details is WORST because it still shares their confidential experience without consent.

deeperInsight: Changing details doesn’t create consent; only the client can grant that.

scenario: In employer-sponsored coaching, your client is using the sessions to plan their exit from that same employer.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Report it to the sponsor who’s paying
Coach the client’s genuine agenda while honoring the confidentiality terms you all set
Refuse to discuss anything about leaving
Subtly steer them toward staying

explanation.best: Coaching the client’s real agenda within the agreed confidentiality is BEST — the client, not the sponsor, owns the session content.
explanation.worst: Reporting it to the sponsor is WORST because it betrays the client’s confidentiality.

deeperInsight: Sponsorship funds the coaching; it doesn’t entitle the sponsor to what the client works on.

scenario: A client wants your help building the strategy for an active lawsuit against a former business partner.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Help them plan the legal strategy
Coach what matters to them and refer legal strategy to their attorney
Tell them how you’d handle the case
Advise them to just settle

explanation.best: Coaching what matters to them and referring legal strategy to their attorney is BEST — legal strategy is outside coaching.
explanation.worst: Telling them how you’d handle the case is WORST because it’s giving legal counsel you’re not qualified to give.

deeperInsight: Coaching clarifies what the client wants; legal strategy belongs to their lawyer.

scenario: A client asks you to email their prospective employer personally vouching that they’re ready for a senior role.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Send the endorsement to help them land it
Clarify that vouching isn’t the coaching role, and coach them to make their own case
Send a vague but positive note
Send it in exchange for a testimonial

explanation.best: Coaching them to make their own case is BEST — personally vouching steps outside the coaching role.
explanation.worst: Sending an endorsement in exchange for a testimonial is WORST because it trades favors and compromises both.

deeperInsight: Coaching builds the client’s ability to represent themselves; it doesn’t become their advocate.

scenario: Session after session, your client uses the time purely to vent, resisting any move toward what they want to do about it.
question: Select the BEST and WORST actions:
options: Let them keep venting indefinitely
